performers: Musopen Symphony, as credited on Wikimedia Commons; conductor not named
intro: Borodin’s orchestral picture of a caravan crossing the steppe, written in 1880 and dedicated to Liszt. It is built on a Russian song and an Eastern melody, which are heard separately and then played together.

sections.label: A · Russian song over violin harmonics
B · Cor anglais and cellos, letter E
sections.mNote: The cellos share the melody with the cor anglais.

sections.label: D · Letter G, horn over pizzicato strings
Coda · Flute solo and muted violins

cues.title: High violin harmonics
cues.text: The first violins, divided into several parts, hold high harmonics marked pp. A flute enters with long notes at bar 2 and an oboe at bar 4. The harmonics continue beneath the whole opening section.
cues.evidence: Belaieff first edition of the full score (Leipzig, 1880), printed pp. 4–5: divided first violins in harmonics with 8va, pp; flute from bar 2, oboe from bar 4; the harmonics continue to letter A. https://archive.org/details/vsredneiaziimuzy00boro Typeset full score, IMSLP file 1016329 (also file 283781), bars 1–42.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Clarinet theme
cues.text: The first clarinet plays the Russian song at bar 5, marked p cantabile. At sounding pitch it begins E, D, C♯, then B and C♯, and falls to A and E in bar 7.
cues.evidence: Belaieff first edition, printed p. 4: first clarinet in A enters in bar 5, p cantabile. Pitches from the typeset full score, IMSLP file 1016329, bars 5–9, transposed down a minor third to sounding pitch; the bars are quoted on the composer page. https://archive.org/details/vsredneiaziimuzy00boro
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Horn melody, bar 17
cues.text: At bar 17 a horn plays the same melody, again marked p cantabile, while the violins hold their harmonics.
cues.evidence: Belaieff first edition, printed p. 4: horn enters in bar 17, p cantabile, at the end of the first system; the first violins continue their harmonics. https://archive.org/details/vsredneiaziimuzy00boro
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Cor anglais melody
cues.text: At letter A the cor anglais enters with a new melody marked cantabile ed espressivo, over pizzicato violas and cellos. The part is printed with one sharp for an instrument in F, which puts the melody in A minor.
cues.evidence: Belaieff first edition, printed p. 5: letter A, cor anglais cantabile ed espressivo with one sharp in its key signature; violas and cellos pizzicato. https://archive.org/details/vsredneiaziimuzy00boro
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Tableaux vivants scheme, 1879
cues.text: In summer 1879 two men asked Rimsky-Korsakov, Borodin and other composers for music to accompany tableaux vivants marking twenty-five years of Alexander II’s reign. The scheme collapsed, and Borodin’s piece was played at concerts.
cues.evidence: Rimsky-Korsakov, My Musical Life (Knopf, 1923), chapter XV, the passage on the summer of 1879: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/7/72/IMSLP721391-PMLP52433-My_Musical_Life_eng_edt.pdf

cues.title: Horn theme over trombones
cues.text: At letter C two horn parts, marked p, play a theme over the trombones, cellos and basses, and the music builds towards the tutti.
cues.evidence: Belaieff first edition, printed p. 8: letter C, both horn staves p with an accent on the first note, trombones p; the tutti begins at letter D on p. 9. https://archive.org/details/vsredneiaziimuzy00boro
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Full orchestra tutti
cues.text: Winds, brass and strings play accented chords together in a tutti from letter D that ends where the strings change to pizzicato and the winds drop to mf.
cues.evidence: Belaieff first edition, printed pp. 9–11: ff and accents for the full orchestra from letter D; at the top of p. 11 the strings are marked pizz. and the winds mf. https://archive.org/details/vsredneiaziimuzy00boro
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Return of the Eastern melody
cues.text: At letter E the cor anglais plays the melody again, marked p cantabile, and the cellos play it with the bow beneath.
cues.evidence: Belaieff first edition, printed p. 11: letter E, cor anglais p cantabile, cellos arco p cantabile. https://archive.org/details/vsredneiaziimuzy00boro
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Dedication to Liszt
cues.text: At Weimar in June 1881 Borodin wrote to his wife that Liszt was pleased with the Steppes and had urged him to make a four-hand arrangement by the next day. Borodin dedicated the piece to Liszt.
cues.evidence: Alfred Habets, Borodin and Liszt, translated by Rosa Newmarch, part II, letter to Madame Borodin, Weimar, 19 June 1881, pp. 189–192: https://archive.org/details/borodinlisztilif00habe

cues.title: Horn at letter G
cues.text: At letter G a horn enters, marked p cantabile, over pizzicato violas, cellos and basses, as the flutes and violins end the triplet melody of the preceding bars. The critic Soloviev wrote that the Russian and the Eastern theme, at first separate, afterwards unite.
cues.evidence: Belaieff first edition, printed p. 15: flutes and first and second violins with triplet figures in the bars before letter G; at G a horn p cantabile, violas, cellos and basses pizz. Soloviev’s remark is quoted in Habets, Borodin and Liszt, p. 68: https://archive.org/details/borodinlisztilif00habe
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Muted solo violins, flute solo
cues.text: Four solo violins, divided and muted, hold long notes while the first flute plays a solo marked pp cantabile dolcissimo. The score then marks rall. e dim. and p perdendosi, and ends pppp.
cues.evidence: Belaieff first edition, printed p. 17, last system: “4 Soli div. con sord.” in the violins; “1. Solo” in the flute, pp cantabile dolciss.; rall. e dim.; p perdendosi; pppp. https://archive.org/details/vsredneiaziimuzy00boro
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

composer.epithet: Russian chemist, professor at the Medical-Surgical Academy in Saint Petersburg, who composed two symphonies, two string quartets and the opera Prince Igor.
facts: Medical-Surgical Academy, Saint Petersburg, 1850–58; chemistry under Nikolay Zinin; Heidelberg, 1859–61; guidance in composition from Mily Balakirev
Adjunct professor of chemistry at the Academy from 1862, professor from 1864; lecturer at the women’s medical courses from 1872
Balakirev · Mussorgsky · Cui · Rimsky-Korsakov · Stasov · Liszt at Weimar

composer.background:
Alexander Borodin was born in Saint Petersburg on 12 November 1833, which was 31 October in the Russian calendar of the day. His father, Luka Gedianov, was a Georgian prince, and his mother, Avdotya Antonova, a soldier’s daughter. As was usual in such cases, the boy was registered as the son of one of Gedianov’s serfs, Porfiry Borodin. He was taught at home. His first compositions were a flute concerto of 1847 and a trio for two violins and cello on a theme from Meyerbeer’s Robert le diable. With his friend Mikhail Shchiglev he played the symphonies of Haydn, Beethoven and Mendelssohn as piano duets, and he learnt the cello.

In 1850 Borodin entered the Medical-Surgical Academy, and from his third year he worked in the laboratory of the chemist Nikolay Zinin. Zinin named him as his successor and warned him in public that “you make a mistake in hunting two hares at once”. In the autumn of 1856, as a young army surgeon, Borodin met the seventeen-year-old guards officer Mussorgsky at a military hospital. He took his doctorate in medicine in 1858, and in 1859 he was sent abroad for three years, most of them in Heidelberg, where he worked in Erlenmeyer’s laboratory with Mendeleev among his colleagues. In Heidelberg in 1861 he met the pianist Ekaterina Protopopova, who played Schumann and Chopin to him. They married after his return to Saint Petersburg in 1862.
